metadata.title: Predicting problem-solving success in an office simulation applying N-grams and a random forest to behavioral process data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a single-sample, in-person dataset of 234 VET students working in the Luca web-based office simulation; the manuscript does not report the use of complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. Because the analysis is based on machine-learning classification (random forest) trained on log-derived n-gram features, the authors do not describe applying any student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or BRR/jackknife replicate weights. The weighting strategy therefore appears to be omitted, and results should be interpreted as predictive performance for the collected sample rather than population-representative estimates. Preprocessing includes exporting JSON logs, cleaning/aggregating events, restricting to early windows (first 5/10/20 minutes), and removing participants who worked outside the simulation; these steps define the analytic sample used for model training/testing.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper predicts problem-solving success from behavioral log data in a computer-based office simulation, using a rubric-based score that is then dichotomized into two classes; it does not use PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes. The manuscript does not describe any missing-data strategy for predictors or outcomes (e.g., how missing log events, incomplete early windows, or missing rubric components were handled), which is a reporting gap given that log-based datasets commonly contain incomplete traces.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used an in-person sample of 234 VET students who worked on a supplier-selection scenario in the Luca web-based office simulation. Participants were excluded if they worked outside the web-based simulation. Log preprocessing aggregated subsequent events of the same kind into single activities, removed events deemed uninformative by simulation design (e.g., double clicks, closing a tool to open another), and restricted the modeling datasets to early clickstream/keystroke windows (first 5, first 10, and first 20 minutes). For the classification target, rubric sum scores were dichotomized using a cut at 53 points, and borderline cases (n=10) were excluded to create balanced classes.

main_findings.dataset_used: Luca office simulation (VET students) — early process windows (first 5/10/20 minutes)
main_findings.target_variable: Problem-solving success class (more vs less successful)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random forest (M1 <5 min): Accuracy=0.53, F1(less)=0.53, F1(more)=0.53, AUC=0.61. Random forest (M2 <10 min): Accuracy=0.60, F1(less)=0.64, F1(more)=0.56, AUC=0.63. Random forest (M3 <20 min): Accuracy=0.60, F1(less)=0.63, F1(more)=0.57, AUC=0.67. With feature selection (robust features): AUC improved to 0.65 (M1robust), 0.66 (M2robust), and ~0.70 (M3robust).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using Luca office simulation data from VET students’ early log windows, the study leveraged note-taking behavior, spreadsheet calculation behavior, document exploration behavior, and early window length to predict problem-solving success (more vs less successful), finding that predictive discrimination improves as the early window expands (AUC rising from 0.61 at <5 min to 0.67 at <20 min, and to ~0.70 with selected robust bigrams). This indicates that adaptive scaffolding can be triggered later in the process (around 10–20 minutes) using behavioral sequence signals, though the results are sample-specific and the paper does not report a missing-data strategy or survey-weighted generalization.

data.outcome_summary: The study predicts problem-solving success in a computer-based office simulation (Luca) using behavioral process data from VET students (N=234). Success was scored via a rubric across planning, applying, deciding, and communicating, then dichotomized into more vs less successful students using a cut at 53 points while excluding borderline cases (n=10) to balance classes. The authors extracted n-gram features (unigrams and bigrams) from early clickstream/keystroke logs and trained a random forest classifier on three early windows: first 5, 10, and 20 minutes, using a 70/30 train-test split plus 10-fold cross-validation for AUC. Performance improved with longer observation windows (AUC: 0.61 → 0.63 → 0.67; accuracy: 0.53 → 0.60 → 0.60), and feature selection further increased AUC to ~0.70 for the 20-minute window. Limitations include no reported missing-data handling and no discussion of survey weights or hierarchical structure adjustments, so generalization beyond this sample should be cautious.
